questions.stem: Which sequence shows the usual order of stages in early first-language acquisition?
options: cooing, holophrastic, babbling, two-word, telegraphic
babbling, holophrastic, cooing, two-word, telegraphic
cooing, babbling, holophrastic, two-word, telegraphic
babbling, cooing, holophrastic, telegraphic, two-word
questions.explanation: Infants coo with vowel-like sounds before they babble consonant–vowel syllables, then produce single words, two-word combinations and telegraphic speech. Babbling comes after cooing, not before it.

questions.stem: Cooing, the earliest stage of vocal play, consists mainly of:
options: consonant–vowel syllables such as ‘baba’
single words that stand for whole sentences
two-word combinations without inflections
vowel-like sounds such as ‘ooo’ and ‘aaa’
questions.explanation: Cooing produces mainly vowel-like sounds, often with some back consonants, as the baby gains control of the vocal tract. Repeated consonant–vowel syllables are babbling, which follows.

questions.stem: A baby produces strings such as ‘bababa’ and ‘dadada’, repeating the same consonant–vowel syllable. This is called:
options: a holophrase
reduplicated babbling
variegated babbling
cooing
questions.explanation: Reduplicated (canonical) babbling repeats one syllable. Variegated babbling, which tends to come later, varies the consonants and vowels, as in ‘badigu’.

questions.stem: Reaching for a cup, a 14-month-old says ‘juice!’, meaning ‘I want some juice.’ A single word used to express a whole sentence's meaning is called:
options: a holophrase
a telegraphic utterance
an overextension
a babble
questions.explanation: At the holophrastic stage, one word carries the meaning of a whole utterance, and context and intonation do the rest. An overextension is using a word for too wide a range of referents, which is not happening here.

questions.stem: A child says ‘Mummy sock’, which could mean ‘That is Mummy's sock’ or ‘Mummy, put my sock on.’ This shows that at the two-word stage:
options: context is needed to interpret the child's meaning
children already use inflections to mark possession
word order is random and carries no meaning
children produce only nouns and never any verbs at all
questions.explanation: Two-word utterances leave out function words and inflections, so the same pair can express different relationships, and listeners rely on context. The child has not used possessive ’s, so inflection is not marking anything here.

questions.stem: In telegraphic speech such as ‘Mummy drink tea’, the child mainly leaves out:
options: content words such as nouns
the subject of each clause
the stressed syllables of words
function words and inflections
questions.explanation: Like a telegram, telegraphic speech keeps the content words that carry meaning and drops determiners, auxiliaries and inflections such as -ing. The nouns and verb are all present, so content words are not what is missing.

questions.stem: A four-year-old says, ‘When I goed to the park, I seed a dog that was really big.’ Which features show the child is post-telegraphic?
options: subordinate clauses and past-tense inflections
the absence of any over-generalised verb forms
single words carrying whole-sentence meanings
the omission of determiners and auxiliary verbs
questions.explanation: The child uses a subordinate clause (‘when I goed to the park’), a relative clause and past-tense marking, which mark post-telegraphic speech. ‘Goed’ and ‘seed’ are over-generalisations, but they show the regular rule being applied, not a lack of development.

questions.stem: The universal grammar theory of language acquisition was proposed by:
options: Michael Tomasello
Roman Jakobson
Noah Webster
Noam Chomsky
questions.explanation: Chomsky proposed that children are born with innate knowledge of the structure of language. Tomasello is associated with the opposing usage-based account.

questions.stem: According to universal grammar, children:
options: learn grammar mainly through explicit correction by adults
cannot begin to acquire grammar until the critical period ends
are born with innate knowledge of the structure of language
build their grammar from interaction and general cognitive skills
questions.explanation: Universal grammar holds that a set of rules shared by all languages is innate, which prioritises nature over nurture. Building grammar from interaction and general cognition is the usage-based view.

questions.stem: A linguist argues that children hear incomplete, error-filled speech, yet still acquire complex grammar quickly and in similar stages. This argument is used to support:
options: the critical period, as evidence that adults learn faster
code switching, as evidence that children mix two systems
universal grammar, as evidence that some knowledge is innate
usage-based theory, as evidence that input is all children need
questions.explanation: This is the poverty-of-the-stimulus argument: if the input seems too poor to explain what children know, some knowledge may be built in. Usage-based theorists respond that child-directed speech is richer than this argument assumes.

questions.stem: Carers often use slower speech, exaggerated intonation and repeated frames such as ‘Where’s the ___?’, and children's earliest grammar is built around such frames. This evidence best supports:
options: usage-based theory, which stresses input and pattern-finding
universal grammar, which stresses innate grammatical rules
the critical period, which stresses limits set by age
fossilisation, which stresses learner errors that stop changing
questions.explanation: Usage-based accounts emphasise child-directed speech and show children building grammar outward from frames they hear repeatedly. Universal grammar predicts development driven by innate rules rather than by the details of the input.

questions.stem: A toddler says ‘more juice’, ‘more biscuit’ and ‘more swing’, but uses ‘more’ in no other structure. A usage-based account would describe ‘more ___’ as:
options: an item-based construction learned from repeated input
an innate parameter being switched on by experience
a holophrase, because each phrase expresses a single meaning
telegraphic speech missing only an -ing inflection
questions.explanation: Tomasello describes early grammar as item-based: a fixed word with a slot (a pivot schema) learned from what the child hears, before more general patterns form. These are two-word combinations, so they are not holophrases.

questions.stem: Over-generalised forms such as ‘goed’ and ‘mouses’ are used as evidence that children do not simply imitate adults, because:
options: these forms occur only in children who are acquiring two languages
adults rarely say these forms, so children have not heard them
these forms show the child has mastered irregular verbs
these forms appear only after the critical period has ended
questions.explanation: Children produce forms they are unlikely to have heard, which shows they are applying a rule rather than copying. ‘Goed’ shows the irregular verb has not yet been mastered, not that it has.

questions.stem: In VCE English Language, the critical period of language acquisition is:
options: the first year of life, after which no language can be learned at all
the period in adulthood when additional languages are learned fastest
the stage when a child produces telegraphic two- and three-word speech
the time between birth and puberty when language is acquired easily
questions.explanation: The critical period runs from birth to puberty; after it, acquiring grammar is difficult and, for some, never fully achieved. It does not end at one year, since children are still in the early stages then.

questions.stem: Genie was found in California in 1970, aged 13, after years of extreme isolation. She learned many words but never fully mastered English syntax. Her case is used as evidence for:
options: the claim that vocabulary is harder than syntax
the critical period hypothesis
the idea that syntax comes before vocabulary
the view that input alone is enough at any age
questions.explanation: Genie missed language input before puberty and later acquired vocabulary but not full grammar, which fits a critical period for syntax. Her vocabulary grew while her syntax did not, the reverse of syntax coming first.

questions.stem: Why is Genie's case treated with caution as evidence for a critical period?
options: she was isolated for only a few weeks before she was found
her severe abuse and possible other impairments may explain her difficulties
she learned syntax perfectly once she received intensive daily teaching
she had been raised speaking two languages before her isolation began
questions.explanation: Genie's extreme neglect and trauma, and the possibility of a developmental impairment, mean her language problems cannot be put down to age alone. A single case with so many confounding factors cannot prove the hypothesis.

questions.stem: A child is raised from birth hearing Greek from her father and English from her mother. This is an example of:
options: simultaneous bilingualism
sequential bilingualism
an interlanguage
language shift
questions.explanation: Simultaneous bilingualism means acquiring two languages from birth or very early childhood. Sequential bilingualism means learning a second language after the first is established, for example on starting school.

questions.stem: An adult learner of English says, ‘Yesterday I go to shop and buy two apple.’ The learner's developing system, which has its own consistent rules, is called:
options: a sociolect
a lingua franca
an interlanguage
a creole
questions.explanation: An interlanguage is the systematic, changing version of the target language that a learner builds, shaped by the first language and by what has been learned so far. A creole is the first language of a whole community, not one learner's developing system.

questions.stem: A Mandarin-speaking learner of English often says ‘two apple’ and ‘many book’. Linguists would explain this partly as:
options: over-generalisation of the regular -s plural to every English noun
the critical period preventing adults from learning any morphology
semantic broadening of nouns such as ‘apple’ to include plurals
transfer from the first language, which does not inflect nouns like these for plural
questions.explanation: Mandarin does not add a plural inflection to nouns such as ‘apple’ or ‘book’, so the learner transfers this pattern to English. Over-generalisation would add -s where it does not belong, as in ‘sheeps’, which is the opposite of leaving it out.

questions.stem: Many young additional-language learners listen and build understanding for some time before they begin to speak. This is called:
options: the critical period
fossilisation
the silent period
the holophrastic stage
questions.explanation: In the silent period, learners take in the new language and communicate non-verbally before producing speech. The holophrastic stage is a stage of first-language acquisition, when single words carry whole meanings.

questions.stem: Compared with young children, adults learning an additional language usually:
options: acquire the language without any conscious study or instruction
pass through the cooing and babbling stages again
progress faster at first but rarely gain a native-like accent
gain a native-like accent faster than young children usually do
questions.explanation: Adults use their cognitive maturity and literacy to learn vocabulary and rules quickly at first, but after the critical period a native-like accent is rarely achieved. Children who start young tend to reach native-like pronunciation.

questions.stem: A bilingual five-year-old says, ‘Can I have more leche, please?’, using the Spanish word for ‘milk’. In language learning, this is best described as:
options: evidence that the child cannot tell the two languages apart
a sign of a language disorder that needs speech therapy
semantic over-generalisation of the English word ‘milk’
code switching, a normal feature of bilingual development
questions.explanation: Bilingual children routinely draw on both languages, often filling a gap with the word that comes most readily. This is a natural and skilled use of two systems, not confusion between them.

questions.stem: Mai speaks Vietnamese to her grandmother and English at school, and moves between both mid-sentence with her bilingual cousin. This shows that she:
options: adjusts her language choice to her interlocutor and context
has not yet separated her two language systems
is in the process of shifting from English back to Vietnamese
has a Vietnamese interlanguage that is fossilised
questions.explanation: Mai uses one language with monolingual speakers and switches only with someone who shares both, which shows control of two separate systems. If she could not separate them, she would mix them with everyone.

questions.stem: Which pair of English consonants differs only in voicing?
options: /m/ and /n/
/s/ and /z/
/s/ and /ʃ/
/t/ and /s/
questions.explanation: /s/ and /z/ are both alveolar fricatives; /s/ is voiceless and /z/ is voiced. /s/ and /ʃ/ are both voiceless and differ in place of articulation.

questions.stem: The sound /ð/, as at the start of ‘then’, is a voiced:
options: velar fricative
bilabial approximant
dental fricative
alveolar stop
questions.explanation: /ð/ is made with the tongue against the upper teeth and a continuous, turbulent airflow, with the vocal folds vibrating. The voiceless dental fricative is /θ/, as in ‘thin’.

questions.stem: The consonants /m/, /n/ and /ŋ/ share which manner of articulation?
options: nasal
affricate
fricative
lateral approximant
questions.explanation: For nasals, the mouth is blocked and the velum is lowered so air flows out through the nose. They differ in place: bilabial, alveolar and velar.

questions.stem: The final sound in ‘sing’, /ŋ/, is made by raising the back of the tongue against the soft palate. Its place of articulation is:
options: velar
alveolar
palatal
glottal
questions.explanation: The soft palate is the velum, so /ŋ/ is a velar nasal, made in the same place as /k/ and /g/. Alveolar sounds such as /n/ are made at the ridge behind the top teeth.

questions.stem: Vowels are classified by:
options: tongue height, tongue backness and lip rounding
voicing, place and manner of articulation
pitch, stress, volume and tempo
alliteration, assonance and rhyme
questions.explanation: Vowels are made without obstruction, so they are described by where the tongue is and the shape of the lips. Voicing, place and manner are used to classify consonants.

questions.stem: Using the Australian English transcription system, which IPA transcription represents the word ‘shed’?
options: /sed/
/ʒed/
/tʃed/
/ʃed/
questions.explanation: ‘Shed’ begins with the voiceless postalveolar fricative /ʃ/ and has the vowel /e/. /ʒ/ is its voiced counterpart, heard in the middle of ‘measure’, and /tʃ/ is the affricate in ‘chip’.

questions.stem: Which word begins with the voiceless sound /θ/?
options: this
they
thin
then
questions.explanation: ‘Thin’ begins with voiceless /θ/. ‘Then’, ‘this’ and ‘they’ begin with the voiced /ð/, even though all four are spelt with ‘th’.

questions.stem: Linguists use the IPA rather than ordinary spelling to record children's speech because:
options: English spelling does not represent sounds consistently
the IPA shows the meaning of every word as well as its sound
children's speech cannot be written in letters of any kind
the IPA records only the errors that children make
questions.explanation: In English one sound can be spelt many ways and one spelling can represent several sounds, as ‘th’ does in ‘thin’ and ‘then’. The IPA gives one symbol for each distinctive sound, so speech is recorded accurately.

questions.stem: A child pronounces ‘then’ /ðen/ as [den]. Which phonological process is this?
options: gliding: a liquid is replaced by a glide
cluster reduction: one consonant is dropped
stopping: a fricative is replaced by a stop
fronting: a velar is replaced by an alveolar
questions.explanation: The fricative /ð/ is replaced by the stop /d/, made in a similar place. Fronting moves a sound forward in the mouth, as when /k/ becomes /t/.

questions.stem: A child pronounces ‘get’ /get/ as [det]. Which phonological process is this?
options: stopping: a fricative is replaced by a stop
final consonant deletion: the last sound is lost
assimilation: one sound becomes like another
fronting: a velar is replaced by an alveolar
questions.explanation: Velar /g/ is replaced by alveolar /d/, which is further forward in the mouth. Both are stops, so this is not stopping.

questions.stem: A child says ‘wabbit’ for ‘rabbit’ and ‘yeyo’ for ‘yellow’. Which phonological process is this?
options: stopping
fronting
cluster reduction
gliding
questions.explanation: In gliding, the liquids /r/ and /l/ are replaced by the glides /w/ and /j/. The words have no clusters, and no fricatives are replaced by stops.

questions.stem: A child says ‘tup’ for ‘cup’, ‘doe’ for ‘go’ and ‘tea’ for ‘key’, but says ‘sun’ and ‘fish’ correctly. Which description best accounts for these data?
options: the velar stops /k/ and /g/ are fronted to alveolar /t/ and /d/
the initial fricatives in each word are replaced by stops
the voiced stops at the start of words become voiceless
the final consonants in each word are consistently deleted
questions.explanation: Every error replaces a velar with an alveolar stop, while fricatives such as /s/ and /f/ are correct, so this is velar fronting. ‘Go’ becoming ‘doe’ keeps voicing, so devoicing does not fit.

questions.stem: A child said ‘went’ at age two, ‘goed’ at three and ‘went’ again at four. The best explanation for the middle stage is that the child:
options: has learned the regular past-tense rule and is applying it widely
has forgotten the word ‘went’ and is guessing at random
is imitating the past-tense forms used by adults
has regressed to an earlier stage of acquisition
questions.explanation: Early ‘went’ is learned as a whole word; ‘goed’ shows the child has worked out the -ed rule and is over-generalising it, before learning the exception. This is progress, not regression, which is why it is called U-shaped development.

questions.stem: Which inflection typically appears earliest in the speech of children acquiring English?
options: third-person singular -s, as in ‘she runs’
contracted auxiliary, as in ‘she’s running’
present progressive -ing, as in ‘running’
regular past tense -ed, as in ‘jumped’
questions.explanation: Studies of English-speaking children, beginning with Roger Brown's, find that -ing appears first among grammatical morphemes. Regular past -ed and third-person -s come later, and contracted auxiliaries are among the last.

questions.stem: A toddler calls every four-legged animal, including cats and cows, ‘doggie’. This is:
options: semantic underextension of the word ‘doggie’
morphological over-generalisation of a suffix
a hypocoristic form used for affection
semantic over-generalisation (overextension)
questions.explanation: The child extends the word to referents that share a feature, four legs, with the original meaning. Underextension is the opposite, as when ‘shoe’ is used only for the child's own shoes.

questions.stem: Children's negatives often develop from ‘No go bed’ to ‘I no go bed’ to ‘I don’t want to go to bed.’ This sequence shows that:
options: negation is acquired only once the critical period has ended
the earliest negatives are formed by adding the suffix -n’t
the negative moves inside the clause and auxiliaries are added
children copy adult negatives correctly from the very start
questions.explanation: At first ‘no’ is attached to the front of the utterance; next it moves inside, after the subject; finally the child uses an auxiliary such as ‘do’ with -n’t. The early forms are not adult-like, so children are not simply copying.

questions.stem: A child moves from ‘Where Daddy going?’ to ‘Where is Daddy going?’ The later form shows the child has acquired:
options: the plural inflection on nouns
the passive voice, with ‘Daddy’ as the agent
coordinating conjunctions such as ‘and’ and ‘but’
auxiliary verbs and subject–auxiliary inversion
questions.explanation: The auxiliary ‘is’ now appears, placed before the subject, which is how English forms questions. Nothing in the change involves plurals, the passive or conjunctions.

questions.stem: Before recording a six-year-old for a field work study, a student researcher must obtain:
options: nothing, as long as names are left out
informed consent from a parent or guardian
consent only from the child's teacher
permission after the recording is made
questions.explanation: A child cannot give informed consent alone, so a parent or guardian must agree after being told the purpose and use of the data; the child's own agreement should be sought too. Removing names protects privacy but does not replace consent.

questions.stem: A student notices that a child speaks much less naturally whenever the microphone is in view. This problem in linguistic field work is called:
options: language shift
the silent period
the observer's paradox
the critical period
questions.explanation: The observer's paradox is that researchers want to record natural speech, but being observed changes how people speak. Discreet recording equipment and longer sessions help reduce it.

questions.stem: Partway through a study, a participant says she no longer wants her recording used. The researcher should:
options: ask her parent or employer to override her decision
remove and delete her data, because consent can be withdrawn
keep the data, because she signed a consent form at the start
keep the data, but give her a pseudonym in the final report
questions.explanation: Informed consent includes the right to withdraw at any time, so her data must not be used. A pseudonym protects identity but does not make it acceptable to use data she has withdrawn.
